description: Delaney's two-act kitchen-sink drama, framed by Helen's arrivals and departures from Jo's life.
content_html:
A Play Built Around One Room

A Taste of Honey takes place almost entirely in a single rented flat in Salford — damp walls, sparse furniture, a view of nothing in particular. This single-setting approach is one of Shelagh Delaney’s most powerful structural choices. The world beyond the flat is real but unreachable: Peter’s car, the canal, the fairground, the docks where the Boy’s ship is moored — all of it exists only as something characters come from or disappear to. As a designer, you might use a set design that makes the flat feel cramped and trapped: low ceilings implied by low borders, a single practical window through which light changes with the seasons, peeling wallpaper as a visual symbol of neglect.

Key Fact

The play is set entirely in a rented flat in Salford, Lancashire, in the late 1950s. The single, unchanging location keeps the audience focused on relationships and traps Jo and Helen in their circumstances — escape is something that only happens off-stage.

The Two-Act Structure

The play divides into two acts separated by the passage of roughly six months. Act One takes place in winter: Helen and Jo arrive at the flat, Helen departs with Peter, and Jo begins her brief relationship with the Boy before he sails away. Act Two takes place in spring and summer: Jo is pregnant, Geof moves in to help her, and eventually Helen returns and Geof is forced out. The structure is symmetrical in a bleak way — the play begins with a departure (Helen leaves Jo for Peter) and ends with a departure (Geof leaves Jo for good), leaving Jo and Helen alone together just as they began.

This circularity is Delaney’s signal to the audience that nothing has fundamentally changed. Jo has not escaped the cycle her mother modelled. A director staging this structural irony might use identical blocking at the opening and the close — Jo in the same position by the window, light at the same low winter angle — so the audience recognises the echo visually.

Kitchen-sink drama is a movement that emerged in British theatre in 1956–1959, placing working-class characters in domestic spaces at the centre of the action. Before this shift, the mainstream British stage was dominated by drawing-room comedies and upper-middle-class settings. John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) and A Taste of Honey (1958) were its two landmark texts.

For a designer, the kitchen-sink aesthetic demands authentic poverty: crockery that is chipped rather than matched, a gas ring rather than a full cooker, curtains that don’t quite reach. Props become symbols of economic reality. Costume choices reinforce class position: Jo’s school coat worn past the point of childhood, Helen’s attempts at glamour with second-hand accessories. A prop as symbol — such as the cheap ring the Boy gives Jo — communicates both affection and precarity in a single moment.

The Role of the Jazz Musicians

One of the most distinctive structural devices in A Taste of Honey is the presence of live jazz musicians on stage throughout the performance. This was added by Joan Littlewood’s Theatre Workshop during rehearsal — it was not in Delaney’s original script — and it draws directly on Brechtian practice. The musicians comment on the action, punctuate scene transitions and prevent the audience from ever fully forgetting that they are in a theatre watching a play. This breaks the fourth wall and creates a presentational quality sitting alongside the naturalistic domestic content.

Key Fact

Live jazz musicians on stage was a Theatre Workshop addition, not in Delaney’s original script. They comment on the action, mark transitions between scenes and create a Brechtian distance that prevents the play from becoming pure naturalism.

Staging Configuration and Space

The original premiere at Theatre Royal Stratford East used a proscenium arch configuration. For a 21st-century production, directors have choices that alter meaning. A thrust or in-the-round configuration would place the audience in closer proximity to Jo’s cramped flat, making the poverty and intimacy of the scenes between Jo and Geof intensely felt. Positioning the jazz musicians upstage in a proscenium staging keeps them visible but separate, emphasising their role as commentators rather than participants. In a thrust configuration, musicians placed to the side could feel more embedded in the world of the play, blurring their Brechtian function.

A common mistake is to describe A Taste of Honey as a purely naturalistic play. The domestic setting, dialect speech and psychological truth of the characters are naturalistic, but the jazz musicians, the moments of direct address to the audience, and the tonal swings from comedy into pathos are all presentational or Brechtian in character. Examiners reward students who identify this hybrid form and discuss how the two modes create meaning together.

A designer staging the hybrid form might keep the set itself firmly realistic — a literally rendered damp flat — while using lighting states that become stylised at key moments: a cool blue wash for the scene by the canal, a harsh white special on Jo when she realises she is pregnant, warmth flooding the stage only during the few scenes when Geof and Jo are at peace together. This contrast between naturalistic set and expressive lighting communicates the emotional temperature to the audience without changing a single piece of furniture.
exam_tip_html: For questions asking you to analyse a playwright’s intentions, the most common mistake is describing the plot — what happens — rather than analysing why Delaney structured the play in a particular way and what she wants the audience to think or feel. For the 12-mark question on intentions, always ask yourself: what does this structural choice make the audience understand about Jo’s situation? For example, the circular two-act structure does not just describe events — it argues that Jo is trapped in a cycle of poverty and neglect. For the 20-mark extended staging response, remember to address both performer and designer choices: name a specific vocal quality or gesture AND a specific lighting state, sound cue or set element, anchoring both to a named moment of the play.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The two-act structure mirrors a cycle: Act One ends with Jo abandoned; Act Two ends with Jo abandoned again — Delaney uses the shape of the play to argue that poverty and neglect repeat themselves.
  • The single-setting flat and kitchen-sink aesthetic are deliberate design choices that trap the audience with Jo and make escape feel impossible — a designer should emphasise cramped space, seasonal light changes and symbolic props.
  • The live jazz musicians are a Brechtian device added by Theatre Workshop, creating a hybrid form: naturalistic domestic content sitting alongside presentational commentary. Recognising this hybrid is essential for top-band answers.

practice_questions.text: Identify the setting in which almost all the action of A Taste of Honey takes place.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a rented flat / a bedsit / a damp flat in Salford. Accept any specific reference to the flat/bedsit in Salford.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'kitchen-sink drama'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a British theatre movement from the late 1950s; 1 mark for explaining that it placed working-class characters and domestic settings at the centre of drama, replacing upper-middle-class drawing-room subjects.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the single-setting flat to communicate Jo's situation to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the single-setting device (1), explanation of how it creates a sense of entrapment or poverty (1), reference to a specific staging or design element that reinforces this (1), link to the audience's understanding of Jo's circumstances or the play's themes (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the live jazz musicians on stage contribute to the audience's experience of the play's structure.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the jazz musicians as a Theatre Workshop / Brechtian device (1), explanation of their structural role in marking scene transitions or commenting on action (1), explanation of how they prevent the audience from fully immersing in naturalism (1), link to their effect on the audience's relationship with the story or characters (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Delaney uses the two-act structure of A Taste of Honey to communicate her intentions about Jo's situation and the cycle of poverty and neglect. Refer to specific moments in the play's structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis of how the circular two-act structure (both acts ending with Jo abandoned) communicates a deliberate argument about cycles of poverty and neglect; identifies the symmetry between Act One's end and Act Two's end; discusses at least one specific structural moment (e.g. the opening and closing mirroring each other) and explains the intended effect on the audience with precision; may reference the Brechtian influence of Theatre Workshop.

Secure: Clear analysis of the two-act structure with reference to at least two moments; understands that Delaney intends an argument not just a story; generally accurate effect on audience identified.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly descriptive; identifies the circular structure but does not fully explain the intention; effect on audience vague.

Emerging: Basic description of what happens in each act; little or no analysis of Delaney's intentions.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging A Taste of Honey, explain how you would use set design, lighting and the positioning of the jazz musicians to communicate to the audience the contrast between the naturalistic domestic world of the flat and the presentational, Brechtian quality of the live music. Refer to specific moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed, concrete staging across set design, lighting and musician positioning; each choice is anchored to a named moment (e.g. the opening arrival, the canal scene, Geof's exit) with a specific effect on the audience stated; discusses the hybrid naturalistic-Brechtian form intelligently; set design choices are specific (materials, levels, props as symbols); lighting choices include lantern types, colour, state changes; musician placement considers sightlines and the Brechtian function; shows clear directorial intention throughout.

Secure: Most design areas covered; at least one named moment per design discipline; generally concrete choices; effect on audience identified in most cases; some sense of the hybrid form.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic ('dark lighting for sad scenes'); few named moments; limited engagement with the Brechtian-naturalistic tension.

Emerging: Basic listing of staging ideas with little justification; no named moments; descriptive rather than analytical.

flashcard_questions.a: A damp rented flat in Salford, Lancashire.

A late-1950s British theatre movement centring working-class characters in domestic settings.

flashcard_questions.q: What structural irony closes A Taste of Honey?
flashcard_questions.a: Jo is left alone with Helen, just as she was at the start — the cycle repeats.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the fourth wall in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The imaginary boundary between the stage world and the audience.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a proscenium arch theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: A traditional configuration with a picture-frame stage and audience seated facing it.

flashcard_questions.q: A Taste of Honey premiered at which theatre?

flashcard_questions.a: The director's planned physical arrangement of actors in space on stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes a style that represents everyday life as closely as possible on stage?
Name one play often cited alongside A Taste of Honey as a founding text of kitchen-sink drama.
flashcard_questions.a: Look Back in Anger by John Osborne (1956).

glossary_terms.definition: The scenery, furniture and physical environment built or arranged on stage to represent a location.
The overall shape of a play, including how it divides into acts and scenes and the pattern of rising and falling action.
The physical arrangement of actors in space on stage, including their positions and movements, planned by the director.
A movement in British theatre from the late 1950s that placed working-class characters and domestic settings at the centre of drama, rejecting drawing-room comedy and middle-class subject matter.
A pioneering British theatre director who led Theatre Workshop and championed working-class voices, collective creation and physical performance.
The imaginary boundary between the stage world and the audience, which naturalistic theatre treats as invisible.
An object used on stage that carries symbolic meaning beyond its literal function.
A traditional theatre configuration with a picture-frame stage framed by an arch, with the audience seated in a single block facing it.
A style of theatre that aims to represent everyday life as closely as possible, using detailed realistic settings and psychologically truthful performances.
The overall quality and colour of the light illuminating the stage at a given moment, set and adjusted by the lighting board operator.
The area of the stage furthest from the audience.
